description: The four margas (jnana, bhakti, karma and raja yoga); varnashramadharma; svadharma, sewa and dana.
content_html:
Four Paths to Liberation

In Hinduism, the four margas are the recognised routes through which a Hindu may seek moksha. The Sanskrit word marga means “path” or “way.” Hindu teaching holds that different people have different temperaments, capacities and stages of life — so more than one path is valid, and a practitioner may follow several simultaneously. The Bhagavad Gita is the primary scriptural source for all four margas, addressed by the god Krishna to the warrior Arjuna.

Key Fact

The four margas are: Jnana yoga (the path of knowledge), Bhakti yoga (the path of devotion), Karma yoga (the path of selfless action) and Raja yoga (the path of meditation and mental discipline). Together they are called Varnashramadharma when understood within the framework of social duty.

Jnana Yoga: The Path of Knowledge

Jnana yoga is the path of wisdom and philosophical enquiry. It involves studying scripture, reasoning and meditating on the relationship between the individual self (atman) and the ultimate reality (Brahman). Jnana yogis study texts such as the Upanishads to see through the illusions of maya and recognise that the self is ultimately identical with Brahman. This is an intellectually demanding path often described as suited to those of a contemplative nature. The Bhagavad Gita at III 29 and 38–41 contrasts those bound by ignorance with those who have purified their understanding.

Through consistent practice, the jnana yogi moves from intellectual understanding to direct experiential realisation of Brahman. This realisation dissolves the false sense of a separate, individual ego. In Advaita Vedanta, the non-dualist school associated with Adi Shankaracharya, jnana is considered the highest path because it directly confronts and dissolves the ignorance (avidya) that perpetuates samsara.

Bhakti Yoga: The Path of Devotion

Bhakti yoga is perhaps the most widely followed path in popular Hinduism. It centres on developing an intense personal love and devotion for a chosen deity (ishta devata). Devotional practices include singing bhajans (devotional hymns), performing puja (ritual worship), chanting the names of God, going on pilgrimage and reading sacred texts such as the Bhagavata Purana. The Bhagavad Gita at IX 26–28 presents bhakti in Krishna’s own words: he teaches that offering even a leaf, flower, fruit or water with devotion and a pure heart is acceptable to him.

Unlike jnana, which requires philosophical study, bhakti is considered accessible to everyone regardless of caste, gender or learning. The medieval poet-saints of the Bhakti Movement — such as Mirabai, Tukaram and Kabir — emphasised that a sincere heart matters more than ritual correctness. Many Hindus combine bhakti with other margas; for example, a devotee may sing bhajans (bhakti) while also performing acts of service (karma yoga).

Some students assume bhakti yoga is a “lower” or simpler form of practice compared with jnana. This is a misconception. Within traditions such as Vaishnavism (devotion to Vishnu/Krishna) and the school of the philosopher Ramanuja, bhakti is the supreme path — even the jnana-achieved insight that the self and Brahman are one is seen as deepening rather than replacing devotion. Ramanuja’s Vishishtadvaita Vedanta argues that the individual self remains distinct from but part of Brahman, and that loving relationship is therefore the ultimate spiritual reality.

Karma Yoga: The Path of Selfless Action

Karma yoga is the path of right and selfless action. Its foundational teaching appears in Bhagavad Gita II 47: “You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions.” The karma yogi acts in the world — working, serving, fulfilling responsibilities — but does so without craving reward or fearing failure. Actions performed in this spirit do not generate the karmic residue that ties a person to samsara.

Karma yoga resonates with the Hindu concept of svadharma — the duties specific to one’s own situation in life. The Bhagavad Gita teaches that it is better to perform one’s own duty imperfectly than to perform another’s duty perfectly. Mahatma Gandhi drew deeply on the karma yoga ideal, describing his political and social work as desireless service (nishkam karma) offered to God rather than a pursuit of personal or political gain.

Raja Yoga: The Path of Meditation

Raja yoga, also called Astanga yoga (eight-limbed yoga), is the path of mental control and meditation. It is most fully outlined in Patanjali’s Yoga Sutras, which describe eight progressive stages: ethical restraint (yama), personal observance (niyama), posture (asana), breath control (pranayama), withdrawal of senses (pratyahara), concentration (dharana), meditation (dhyana) and absorption (samadhi). The Bhagavad Gita at VI 5–7 teaches that through the disciplined mind, a person becomes their own best friend; through an undisciplined mind, their own worst enemy.

Key Fact

Patanjali’s Yoga Sutras outline raja yoga in eight stages. The highest stage, samadhi, is a state of total absorption in which the meditator experiences unity with Brahman. This is the closest the individual comes to moksha whilst still alive — the state Hinduism calls jivan mukti.

Varnashramadharma

Varnashramadharma means the dharma appropriate to one’s varna (social grouping) and ashrama (stage of life). The four traditional ashramas are: student (brahmacharya), householder (grihastha), forest dweller or retiree (vanaprastha) and renunciant (sannyasa). Each stage has its own duties and spiritual emphases — a student is expected to study and practise self-discipline, a householder to fulfil family and social obligations, a retiree to begin withdrawing from worldly concerns, and a renunciant to focus entirely on liberation. The four margas can be seen as suited to different stages: bhakti and karma yoga are particularly prominent in the householder stage, while jnana and raja yoga may deepen in the later stages.

Hindu thinkers have debated whether varnashramadharma is a fixed cosmic order or a flexible social ideal. Some traditional schools treat the four varnas (Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya, Shudra) as describing spiritual qualities rather than hereditary birth categories. The Bhagavad Gita presents Krishna as saying that the four varnas were created by him according to qualities and actions — not birth alone. Modern Hindu reformers such as Swami Vivekananda emphasised that all four varnas are spiritually equal, each serving a necessary function in society.

Sewa (service) is the practical expression of karma yoga in the community. It includes volunteering, running food banks, caring for the sick and elderly, and supporting temples. Organisations such as Sewa International UK coordinate large-scale disaster relief and community service programmes rooted explicitly in the Hindu ideal of selfless service. Dana (giving) is one of the three core religious duties in Hinduism alongside yajna (sacrifice/ritual) and tapas (austerity). Together, sewa and dana reflect the karma yoga principle: act for others without expecting personal reward, and the action purifies rather than binds.
exam_tip_html: The 15-mark Discuss questions on this topic often ask whether one marga is more important than others, or whether selfless action or devotion is the best path to moksha. When you Discuss, present both sides: for example, jnana yoga proponents argue that wisdom directly removes the ignorance causing samsara, while bhakti traditions (especially Ramanuja) counter that love for God is the highest form of realisation. Name specific sources — Bhagavad Gita II 47 for karma yoga, IX 26–28 for bhakti yoga — to access the top mark band. A common student error is treating the four margas as mutually exclusive; examiners reward candidates who show that Hinduism allows — even encourages — following more than one simultaneously. Check the spelling of technical terms: varnashramadharma, svadharma, moksha and nishkam karma are all assessed in SPaG on the extended response.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The four margas — jnana (knowledge), bhakti (devotion), karma (selfless action) and raja/astanga (meditation) — are distinct but complementary paths to moksha, each suited to different temperaments.
  • Karma yoga, anchored in Bhagavad Gita II 47, teaches that right action performed without attachment to results does not bind the actor to samsara — a principle Gandhi applied in his political life.
  • Varnashramadharma links individual duty (svadharma) to social role (varna) and life stage (ashrama). Sewa (service) and dana (giving) are its practical expressions in the community.

practice_questions.text: State one of the four margas in Hinduism.
practice_questions.marks:
Any one of the following for 1 mark:
• Jnana yoga (the path of knowledge)
• Bhakti yoga (the path of devotion)
• Karma yoga (the path of selfless action)
• Raja yoga / Astanga yoga (the path of meditation)
[1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Describe what is meant by karma yoga.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Karma yoga is the path of selfless or desireless action.
• The practitioner fulfils their duties without attachment to the results of those actions.
• It is based on the teaching in Bhagavad Gita II 47 that one has a right to action but not to its fruits.
• Actions performed this way do not generate karma that binds the person to samsara.
[1 mark for a basic description; 2 marks for a developed description that includes the idea of non-attachment or links to karma/samsara.]

practice_questions.text: Outline the meaning of varnashramadharma for Hindus.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Varnashramadharma combines varna (social grouping) and ashrama (stage of life) with dharma (duty).
• It defines the specific duties a Hindu should follow according to their social role and life stage.
• The four ashramas are: student, householder, forest dweller/retiree, and renunciant.
• Different margas are associated with different ashramas: e.g. karma yoga in the householder stage, raja yoga in the renunciant stage.
• Different traditions interpret varna either as hereditary birth categories or as descriptions of spiritual qualities.
[1 mark for a basic outline; 2 marks for some development; 3 marks for a clear, developed outline that names specific ashramas or links to a second concept.]

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways in which the four margas reflect Hindu beliefs about the path to moksha.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Jnana yoga reflects the belief that ignorance (avidya) about the true nature of reality is the root cause of rebirth in samsara. By studying scripture and meditating on the relationship between atman and Brahman, the jnana yogi dissolves this ignorance and achieves liberation. This path is supported by the Upanishads and by the Advaita Vedanta of Shankaracharya.
• Bhakti yoga reflects the belief that loving surrender to God can lead to moksha. Bhagavad Gita IX 26-28 teaches that Krishna accepts sincere devotion from all, regardless of caste or gender, suggesting that moksha is not restricted to the learned but is accessible to all through the heart.
• Karma yoga reflects the belief that action itself is not the problem — it is selfish desire attached to action that binds one to samsara. Bhagavad Gita II 47 teaches that desireless action (nishkam karma) does not accumulate karma and therefore moves the actor towards moksha.
• Raja yoga reflects the belief that the mind must be stilled through meditation to perceive the true self. Samadhi, the highest stage of Patanjali's eight-limbed path, is the experiential union with Brahman that constitutes moksha whilst still living.
[6 marks: up to 3 marks per way — 1 for identifying the marga, 2 for explaining the connection to moksha, 3 for developing the explanation with a named source or concept.]

practice_questions.text: 'Bhakti yoga is the most important path to moksha in Hinduism.' Discuss.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• Bhakti yoga is the most widely practised marga in popular Hinduism, suggesting it resonates most deeply with the majority of believers. Temples, festivals and devotional singing (bhajan and kirtan) all express bhakti.
• Bhagavad Gita IX 26-28 presents Krishna as personally welcoming bhakti: he teaches that offering even simple gifts with devotion is acceptable, implying bhakti is the most direct relationship with the divine.
• The Vaishnavite philosopher Ramanuja argued that bhakti is the highest path because it maintains a loving relationship between the self and Brahman rather than dissolving the self. For Ramanuja, this personal relationship is the ultimate spiritual reality.
• The medieval Bhakti Movement (Mirabai, Tukaram, Kabir) showed that bhakti crosses caste and gender barriers, making it the most inclusive and therefore most universally important path.

Arguments against:
• Jnana yoga tradition, especially Advaita Vedanta (Shankaracharya), holds that knowledge is the highest path because it directly removes avidya (ignorance), the root cause of samsara. Devotion is valuable but remains within the world of maya until knowledge transcends it.
• Karma yoga, as taught in Bhagavad Gita II 47 and lived by Gandhi, can be argued to be most important because it engages with the world rather than withdrawing from it. Social action (sewa, dana) expresses Hindu values in everyday life.
• Raja yoga’s goal of samadhi (direct experiential union with Brahman) could be seen as the most complete realisation of moksha, surpassing even devotion in depth.
• Hindu teaching broadly accepts that all four margas are equally valid and that the idea of one being “most important” misrepresents the tradition’s inclusive approach to liberation.

Mastering: Both sides developed with named sources (Bhagavad Gita II 47; IX 26-28; Ramanuja; Shankaracharya); explicit comparison of margas; a reasoned, justified conclusion that engages with the word “most important.”
Secure: Two clear sides with some development; at least one named source; a conclusion that takes a position.
Developing: One side better developed than the other; limited source use; a partial conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided or very brief; no or incorrect sources; no real conclusion.
[15 marks; SPaG assessed]

practice_questions.text: Outline the meaning of svadharma and explain how it relates to karma yoga.
practice_questions.marks:
Students may include:
• Svadharma means personal or individual duty — the specific obligations appropriate to one’s own social role, life stage and spiritual capacity.
• Karma yoga teaches that performing one’s own duties without attachment to the results does not bind the actor to samsara.
• Bhagavad Gita II 47 states: ‘You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions.’
• Together, svadharma and karma yoga mean that every person has a unique set of duties, and fulfilling those duties selflessly is itself a spiritual path.
[1 mark for a basic outline; 2 marks for linking svadharma to karma yoga; 3 marks for a developed answer that includes a source or example such as Gandhi.]

knowledge_checks.q: Which marga is described as 'the path of selfless action'?
Which text contains the teaching 'You have a right to perform your prescribed duties, but you are not entitled to the fruits of your actions'?
The marga focused on meditation and mental discipline, based on Patanjali's eight-limbed system, is called _____ yoga.
_____ means selfless service to others and is a key expression of karma yoga in social life.
Match each marga to its main focus:
right: Wisdom and philosophical study of atman and Brahman
Loving devotion to a personal deity through worship and song
Performing duties without attachment to results

flashcard_questions.a: The path of knowledge; seeking liberation through wisdom and study of atman and Brahman.
The path of loving devotion to a personal deity, expressed through worship, song and surrender.
The path of selfless action; fulfilling duties without craving the fruits of those actions.

flashcard_questions.q: Which verse of the Bhagavad Gita is the key source for karma yoga?
What does Bhagavad Gita IX 26–28 teach about bhakti yoga?
flashcard_questions.a: Krishna accepts sincere devotion from all; even offering a leaf or flower with love pleases him.

flashcard_questions.q: What is raja yoga also known as?
flashcard_questions.a: Astanga yoga — the eight-limbed path of meditation outlined by Patanjali.
The highest stage of raja yoga; a state of total absorption or union with Brahman.
Duty defined by one’s varna (social grouping) and ashrama (stage of life).

flashcard_questions.q: Name the four ashramas (stages of life) in Hinduism.
flashcard_questions.a: Student, householder, forest dweller/retiree and renunciant.
Personal duty — the specific obligations appropriate to one’s own role, stage and capacity.
Selfless service to others; the practical expression of karma yoga in community life.

flashcard_questions.q: Which modern Hindu figure most famously practised karma yoga through political action?
flashcard_questions.a: Mahatma Gandhi, who described his work as nishkam karma — desireless service to God.

glossary_terms.definition: The four spiritual paths in Hinduism — jnana, bhakti, karma and raja yoga — each leading towards moksha.
The path of knowledge and wisdom; seeking liberation through study of scripture and meditation on atman and Brahman.
The path of loving devotion to a personal deity, expressed through worship, prayer, song and surrender.
The path of selfless action; performing one's duties without attachment to results so as not to accumulate karma.
The path of meditation and mental discipline; Patanjali's eight-limbed (Astanga) system culminating in samadhi.
The Hindu system combining varna (social grouping) and ashrama (stage of life) to define an individual's duties.
Personal or individual duty; the specific obligations appropriate to a person's own role, life stage and spiritual capacity.
Selfless service to others; a key expression of karma yoga in social and community life.
Charitable giving; one of the three core religious duties in Hinduism alongside yajna and tapas.
Liberation from the cycle of death and rebirth (samsara); the ultimate spiritual goal in Hinduism.

hero_image_caption: A Hindu devotee lights an oil lamp during puja, symbolising the bhakti path of devotion that is central to Hindu worship.
